summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style overview of the U.S. state of Oklahoma, covering its name origin, statehood, geography, government and judiciary, religion, education, culture, sports, and economy-related infrastructure. It summarizes congressional delegation makeup for the 112th Congress, the arrival of major league basketball in Oklahoma City, and notable museums, festivals, and ballet history. It also describes the state's mountain ranges, population centers, Native American tribal governments, and inland river ports.
one_line: Overview of Oklahoma's history, geography, government, religion, culture, sports and population centers.
key_facts: Oklahoma became the 46th state to enter the union on November 16, 1907.
The name Oklahoma derives from the Choctaw words okla and humma, meaning red people.
Choctaw Chief Allen Wright suggested the name in 1866 during treaty negotiations; it was officially approved in 1890.
Oklahoma covers 69,898 square miles (181,035 km2), with 1,281 square miles of water, making it the 20th largest state.
Thirty-nine Native American tribal governments are based in Oklahoma.
The Oklahoma judiciary includes the Oklahoma Supreme Court, the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals, and 77 District Courts.
Oklahoma City and Tulsa are two of the fifty largest cities in the United States.
Oklahoma City's metropolitan area had 1,252,987 people in 2010, while Tulsa's had 937,478.
The Seattle SuperSonics relocated to Oklahoma City in July 2008 and became the Oklahoma City Thunder for the 2008–09 season, the state's first permanent major league franchise.
The New Orleans Hornets played two seasons at the Ford Center in Oklahoma City after Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
According to the Pew Research Center, 85 percent of Oklahoma's religious adherents are Christian.
The Sherwin Miller Museum of Jewish Art in Tulsa preserves the largest collection of Jewish art in the Southwest United States.
Cavanal Hill is regarded by the Oklahoma Tourism & Recreation Department as the world's tallest hill at 1,999 feet, one foot short of their mountain definition.
The Five Moons were five Native American ballerinas: Yvonne Chouteau, Marjorie and Maria Tallchief, Rosella Hightower and Moscelyne Larkin.
The Tulsa Port of Catoosa is the most inland ocean-going port in the nation and ships over two million tons of cargo each year.
